# Validate tool input against the registered inputSchema

Issue: re-cinq/HALEngine#37
Labels: priority:medium, type:feature, size:M, area:tools, epic:extension-points

Part of #35

## Why

`ToolRegistry.execute` looks a tool up, logs the input's key names, and calls the executor
without ever checking the declared `inputSchema` (`src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts`).
Every tool declares a JSON Schema (`src/types/ai.ts`) that is handed verbatim to both
providers, but nothing validates what comes back from the model. The shipped example shows the
shape of the problem: `example/weather-tool.ts` declares `location` as a required string, then
casts and defaults it (`(input.location as string) || 'Unknown'`) with a comment warning the reader
that `inputSchema` shapes what the model sends but does not enforce it. That is the careful version,
written by the people who wrote the engine — and it still answers a malformed call with a
confidently formatted forecast for `'Unknown'` rather than telling the model it got the call wrong.

The registry currently pushes this check onto each tool's own executor, leaving every consumer
to implement it itself — differently each time, or not at all. A tool that receives unexpected input must fail
in one predictable, known way before the rest of this epic's tool work can be built on top
of it.

## What to do

Validate `input` against the resolved tool definition's `inputSchema` inside
`ToolRegistry.execute`, before the executor runs, using a JSON Schema validator (`ajv`
unless the build proves otherwise) added to `dependencies` — not a second, hand-written
schema in a different format, since the schema already has to match what is handed to the
providers.

Compile a static tool's schema once at `register` time so a broken schema fails at startup,
not mid-conversation; a schema produced by a function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource`
resolves and compiles per call, cached by the resolved schema object.

A rejection returns a `ToolResponse` (`{result: '<what was wrong>'}`) rather than throwing,
so a malformed call becomes something the model can read and correct within the existing
`DEFAULT_MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS = 5` budget, instead of ending the whole conversation with a
generic transport error. Validation enforces `required`, declared types and `enum` only —
it does not inject `additionalProperties: false`, coerce types, or apply defaults, and
there is no opt-out flag.

Update `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md` and `.specify/spec.md` to match.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against the resolved definition's
      `inputSchema` before calling the executor; on failure it returns a `ToolResponse`
      whose `result` describes the failure, and the executor is never invoked
- [ ] A new `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` (the registry has no test file today)
      registers a tool requiring a `location` string, calls `execute` with `{}`, and
      asserts the returned result names `location` as required and the executor's call
      count is `0`
- [ ] A test asserts valid input with an unlisted extra property is passed through to the
      executor unchanged (`toEqual`, so an added default or coerced value fails the test) —
      exactly once
- [ ] A test asserts a wrong-typed field (a number where a string is required) is rejected
      with a message naming the field path and the expected type, and that the message does
      **not** contain the offending value
- [ ] A test asserts `register` throws at registration time for an uncompilable schema, and
      that the thrown message names the tool
- [ ] A test asserts a function-valued tool definition whose returned schema differs between
      calls is validated against the schema current at that call, not a stale cached one
- [ ] A test asserts a static tool's schema is compiled once across ten `execute` calls
- [ ] A tool-loop test in `chatOrchestrator.test.ts` drives a stub provider through a
      rejected tool call followed by a corrected retry, and asserts `processMessage`
      resolves — not rejects — with the rejection text visible to the provider on the next
      round
- [ ] `execute` still throws `Unknown tool: <name>` for an unregistered name, unchanged,
      pinned by a test
- [ ] Rejection messages and log lines name the failing property paths and the constraint
      that failed, and never a property **value**. Tool input is where identifying data
      enters the engine and the engine redacts nothing today. A test asserts a rejected
      payload containing an identifying field produces no log line and no returned text
      containing that field's value
- [ ] `execute` carries a **one-line** doc comment — `re-lint/max-comment-lines` rejects a
      `@param`/`@returns`/`@throws` block — and the full contract (rejection `ToolResponse` for input
      the schema rejects, throw only for an unknown tool name) is stated in
      `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`, which the comment points at
- [ ] The validator is in `package.json` `dependencies`, not `peerDependencies` or
      `devDependencies`, and
      `npm run build && node --input-type=module -e "import('./dist/index.js')"` exits `0`
- [ ] `README.md` states what the registry now does, and the claim is true rather than
      merely present
- [ ] `docs/adding-a-tool.md` no longer tells executors to cast defensively and handle
      missing input; it states that input reaching an executor has already passed the
      declared schema, that unknown keys may still be present, and that a rejection is
      returned to the model rather than thrown
- [ ] `.specify/spec.md` records that a rejection is a tool result (not an exception), that
      the tool-round bound is what stops a retry cycle from spinning, and that extra
      properties pass through unmodified
- [ ] The PR body states the migration note: an executor that used to hand-validate its
      input now receives only input the schema already accepts, and a tool that relied on
      seeing malformed input to produce its own error message stops seeing it. The version
      bump is MINOR
- [ ] Every test this issue adds cites the statement it validates with an inline
      `([validated by ...])` link in a `specs/**` or `adrs/**` file, and the statements exist
      before the tests do. `re-lint/require-spec-link` fails the build on an uncited test, so the
      spec edits are part of this issue rather than a follow-up
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` carries an entry for this change, written for somebody reading it on npm
      rather than somebody reading this repo's log. CI runs `scripts/check-changelog.sh` and
      fails any PR touching a non-test file under `src/` without one
- [ ] `npm run build`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run eslint` (`--max-warnings 0`)
      and `npm run prettier:check` pass, with no `any` in the changed public surface

## Tech notes

Today's `throw` in `registry.ts` propagates through the orchestrator's tool-call
`Promise.all`, out of the processing loop's `try`, fires `onError`, and reaches the
WebSocket error handler, which sends a generic "Failed to process message" and never sends
the stream-end frame. That end-to-end path is why a rejection has to be a returned
`ToolResponse` instead of a throw.

Deliberately out of scope: the `Unknown tool: <name>` throw stays as-is — the same failure
class handled the opposite way, which is an intentional split, but changing it affects
direct callers and is tracked as *Return an unknown tool name to the model instead of
throwing*. Also out of scope: validating tool *output*; hallucination detection and an
evaluation harness; per-tool authorization — a schema-valid call for someone else's data is still
valid, and authorization is a separate `ToolContext` boundary concern that no issue in this epic
owns (*Let a consumer decline a tool call through a `beforeToolCall` hook* is a veto seam, not an
authorization model); retry, timeout
and rate limiting around tool execution; and any actual tool implementation, which is
written against this contract later.

<document source="AGENTS.md" type="doc" relevance="0.98" tokens="693">
## Spec Header Table

Every `specs/*/spec.md` opens with its title, then a two-column header table,
and carries a lead paragraph of prose before its first `##` section:

```markdown
# <spec title>

| Field  | Value                 |
| ------ | --------------------- |
| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#<n> |
| Status | Draft                 |

<lead paragraph>
```

The lead paragraph does not have to sit immediately after the table: a spec
carrying a metadata block of its own may place that block between the two. What
the convention requires is that prose, rather than a section heading, follows
the header material, and that the prose runs to at least 40 characters -
anything shorter is reported as no lead paragraph at all.

`Issue` names the issue the spec was written against, or `n/a` for the specs
that predate this convention.

`Status` is one of `Draft`, `In Progress` or `Shipped`. It is not a mood, and
it is not a claim about how finished the feature is: it is the spec's own
test-citation coverage. No testable statement cited is `Draft`, some cited is
`In Progress`, all cited is `Shipped`. A spec describing shipped, working
behaviour still reads `Draft` until its statements cite the tests that
validate them.

A spec that should no longer be graded takes a terminal value instead. The
parser buckets roughly sixteen labels into five buckets, and the two terminal
ones skip the coverage check whatever the citation count:

| Written into the spec                                            | Bucket                       |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `Draft`                                                          | `draft`                      |
| `In Progress`, `In Review`, `Planning`, `WIP`, `Proposed`        | `in-progress`                |
| `Shipped`, `Implemented`, `Complete`, `Accepted`, `Done`, `Live` | `shipped`                    |
| `Retired`, `Superseded`, `Removed`, `Deprecated`, `Obsolete`     | `retired` - skips the check  |
| `Rejected`, `Abandoned`                                          | `rejected` - skips the check |

Prefer the canonical `Draft` / `In Progress` / `Shipped` for a live spec; reach
for `Retired` or `Rejected` rather than leaving a superseded spec to claim a
coverage tier it will never earn.

ADRs do not carry this table. They declare their state as YAML frontmatter
`status:` instead - `accepted` for a decision the code implements, `proposed`
for one it does not. That field does mean maturity, which the spec `Status` row
explicitly does not. The difference is deliberate: ADRs are exempt from the
coverage tier, because asking a decision record to cite a test for every
statement it makes is the wrong ask of a decision record.
</document>
<document source="CONTRIBUTING.md" type="doc" relevance="0.55" tokens="610">
## Specs and ADRs

Normative specs are `specs/<slug>/spec.md`, decision records are `adrs/`. Each spec opens with a header table whose **`Status` row tracks test-citation coverage, not how finished the feature is**: no cited statement is `Draft`, some is `In Progress`, all is `Shipped`. A spec describing working, shipped behaviour still reads `Draft` until its statements cite tests. `npm run check:spec-status` enforces the correspondence, so raising `Status` without adding citations fails.

An ADR's `status` is different: that one does mean maturity — `proposed`, `accepted`, `superseded` — and is not a coverage tier.

## What will fail, and why

**Layering.** `src/` is five layers — types → providers → infrastructure → orchestration → transport — declared in `layers.yaml` and enforced by `re-lint/no-cross-layer-import`. A shortcut across them fails lint rather than review, so you find out in seconds instead of in a comment thread.

**Comment length.** A comment may span one line. `re-lint/max-comment-lines` does not exempt JSDoc, and consecutive `//` lines count as one comment. Anything longer belongs in `specs/`, `adrs/` or `docs/`, where it is searchable and linked. Tooling directives are exempt, and an `eslint-disable` may carry its reason after `--`.

**Test traceability.** `re-lint/require-spec-link` wants every test to be cited from a spec or ADR, as `([validated by](path/to/test.ts#L12))` in the statement it validates. A test that validates nothing a spec claims is asking whether it belongs in the traceable suite.

**Documented code blocks.** Every fenced `typescript` block in the ten documents `scripts/check-doc-blocks.mjs` covers (spikes are covered separately: their blocks are opted out wholesale, and one that names a source is reported) carries a marker naming where it comes from — an exported declaration, or a `#region` in a compiled file under `example/`. Run `npm run docs:fix` to regenerate, and read the diff: it will happily delete an annotation the type cannot express. A block that genuinely cannot be generated carries `none -- reason`, and an empty reason fails.

**Changelog.** A pull request that touches non-test files under `src/` must also touch `CHANGELOG.md`. Entries are written for somebody installing the package, not for somebody reading the commit log. The `no-changelog` label is the escape hatch for a change nothing installable can observe, and applying it is a visible act.
</document>
<document source="CLAUDE.md" type="doc" relevance="0.53" tokens="138" truncated="true">
## Specs and ADRs

Normative specs live in `specs/<slug>/spec.md`, decision records in `adrs/`, and the repo-level system spec in `.specify/spec.md`. Research spikes are in `docs/spikes/`; `docs/` otherwise holds how-to guides.

Every spec under `specs/` opens with a header table whose `Status` row tracks its **test-citation coverage**, not how finished the feature is — a spec describing shipped behaviour still reads `Draft` until its statements cite tests. Read AGENTS.md § Spec Header Table and § Spec Test Links before adding or editing a spec.
</document>

# ADR-002: AI Response Validation and Error Classification

This ADR records a proposal to validate AI responses with Zod schemas backed by domain-specific sanity checks, and to classify failures through an explicit decision tree that separates a model hallucinating from a data source returning wrong-but-plausible values. The proposal came out of a proof of concept that returned inaccurate data, where the team could not tell whether the model or the upstream API was at fault. It is **proposed, not adopted**: `package.json` carries no `zod` dependency and `src/` contains no validation layer.

## Consequences

If adopted: a runtime dependency on Zod, schema definitions to maintain alongside the tool registry, and a place in the orchestration layer for validation to live. Sanity checks are domain knowledge, so they cannot ship in a generic engine — they would need to be a pluggable seam, consistent with how `AIProvider` and `SessionStore` already work.
</document>
<document source="adrs/ADR-007-repository-visibility.md" type="adr" relevance="1.00" tokens="628">
## Consequences

- T011 carries `--provenance`; T031's first publish is attested, and the attestation is visible on the registry listing. This ADR is what unblocks both.
- A consumer verifies the result with `npm audit signatures`, which reports how many installed packages carry a verified registry signature and how many carry a verified attestation. That command is the whole consumer-facing benefit of this decision: without a public repository there is no attestation for it to verify, and it reports the package as unattested.
- Secret scanning and push protection become available, and are the backstop against the next accidental credential reaching a repository anyone can read. They are unavailable to an `internal` repository, so enabling them is part of the flip and not something to assume happened: the other public repositories in this scope do not agree on which of the two is on, which is evidence enough that no org-wide default is doing it for us.
- A pull request from a fork receives no repository secrets and a read-only token whatever a workflow's `permissions` block requests. The workflows already account for this; a contributor-facing note is T033's.
- Push access to `main` becomes, transitively, the ability to publish under this scope, because OIDC leaves no stored credential to revoke. Branch protection is the lock and T032 is the alarm behind it; both are dependencies of T031 rather than improvements on it.
- The issue record, the specs and the ADRs - this one included - become public. They are written to be read.
- The repository becomes forkable, and reversal does not recall a fork. Anything that must not be public has to be kept out of a commit rather than removed from one.

# ADR-007: The source repository is public so releases carry provenance

This ADR records that this repository is public, and states the rule a later package should read rather than re-derive: a package published to the public registry from this scope is published with provenance, and a provenance attestation requires a publicly resolvable source repository. The repository was `internal` when this was written; the flip was carried out as a prerequisite of the first release rather than as a step inside it, which is why the measurements below record the state before it.

## Decision

Five sites carry `eslint-disable-next-line` (or, in one case, a file-level `eslint-disable`) with a `--` reason referring here, under the four decisions below. Together they account for every finding these three rules report: run with `--no-inline-config` and the count is three `no-flag-params`, one `prefer-polymorphism` and one `test-imports-its-subject`. The sixth was withdrawn when its rule stopped firing - see the `validateMessage` entry.

**`re-lint/no-flag-params` on `AIError`'s `retryable` parameter** (`src/types/ai.ts`). `AIError` is exported from `src/index.ts` and `retryable` is a `public readonly` constructor parameter, so it is part of the published API. The rule's remedy - split the function into two named functions - means two error classes or two factories, which is a breaking change for every consumer constructing an `AIError`. CLAUDE.md routes breaking changes through an issue, a migration guide, a MINOR bump and a deprecation period; a lint sweep is not that process.

The same constraint reaches every other site that constructs a retryable `AIError`, because `retryable` defaults to `false` and there is no other way to express one. Two carry the same suppression: `mapVertexError` in `src/providers/vertex/vertexProvider.ts`, which classifies a rate limit, an unavailable vendor and a timeout, and one call site in `src/transport/ws/messageHandler.test.ts`, which builds the error a handler is expected to surface. In both the rule's premise is false in the same way - the boolean is not selecting a behaviour, it is a field of a value.
</document>

**dod/otto-176-injection-probe-blocked** (memory): DoD triage for re-cinq/Otto#176 (Probe whether the agent obeys an instruction hidden in a TMS field) => changes_requested / Lore-Dod-Blocked. Branch lore/implementation-loop/issue-176 was level with origin/main (1466fb2); committed only .lore/dod.md (5f425e7) recording the block, no tests.

WHY BLOCKED (verified this run): #176 is a slice ON TOP OF an evaluation harness that does not exist on origin/main. Every acceptance criterion extends pre-existing machinery: "add a probe kind to probes.json", "schema becomes a discriminated union", "the existing groundedness check", "reusing the harness's existing refusal", "extends the harness's existing hash". None of that machinery is in the repo:
- No apps/api/eval/ at all (no grade.ts, groundTruth.ts, agentRun.ts, eval:check, report). Owned by #25 (support-agent-evaluation spec, Draft).
- No probes.json / probes.schema.json. Owned by #46 (support-agent-ai-transparency, Draft).
- No TMS tool registry with declared output fields — only apps/api/src/tools/escalateToHuman exists. TMS tools (case notes, specialInstructions, signerName) owned by #19/#20 (support-agent-tms-tools, Draft). So projection-surface script (FR-067/CR-006) has nothing to read.
- No docs/ dir (no prompt-injection.md, no danish-review.md).

The evaluation spec itself says so: specs/support-agent-evaluation/spec.md L264 ("Nothing from #25 is implemented ... no apps/api/eval/ exists") and L295 ("no apps/api/eval/, docs/ ... None of #14,#17,#19,#20,#21,#22 or #46 is implemented"). Spec status Draft.

So every red test would fail on a missing import/entry point ("no harness/no probes/no tool registry"), NOT on the ticket's own claim (harness never hands the model a tool result arguing with the system prompt). Failing for a reason the ticket never states = changes_requested, not a DoD. Also "really several tickets": #176 cannot precede #25, #46, #19/#20. The Issue Map sequences them in that order.

Ticket also carries a header block on KU-07 (no model selected), which gates the eval:agent half; the "buildable now" parts still need the three foundations first.

Same pattern as [[dod/otto-171-prompt-mask-blocked]] and dod/otto-154-smtp-email-sink-blocked: foundation absent. Lesson: when a ticket says "add X to existing file Y / extend existing harness Z", grep for Y/Z first; if the base spec is Draft and the dir/file is absent, it's blocked-on-foundation, not a DoD.
